title: Calgary high school says too many students are getting food delivered
summary: A Calgary high school sent parents a memo this week asking them to rein in their children’s increasing use of food delivery apps like Uber Eats and DoorDash during school hours.

image.caption: St. Francis High School sent parents a memo Monday outlining concerns about the "increased use of food delivery apps" by students. (Colleen Underwood/CBC)

blocks.text: Calgary·New
A Calgary high school sent parents a memo this week asking them to rein in their children’s increasing use of food delivery apps like Uber Eats and DoorDash during school hours.
St. Francis asks parents to ask kids to stop ordering food during class time

In the letter, St. Francis High School administrators said while the deliveries may be convenient, they can also be disruptive to classrooms, and pose security risks to have students interacting with individuals they don’t know on school grounds.

“As the safety and security of everyone at St. Francis is our priority, we ask that you please have a conversation with your child and ask them to not use any food delivery services during the instructional time of the day," the letter said.

Lee Martin, who represents Calgary Catholic teachers for the Alberta Teachers’ Association, told CBC News it's become more of an issue in recent years. He heard from one teacher just this week who said a driver tried to deliver food right to a classroom window.
“I think that as public educators we want our children fed,” said Martin. “However, this seems to be a bit out of control.”
A food drop-off cart outside an elementary school in Calgary's southeast. (Submitted by Lee Martin)
And it’s not only at high schools.

At one elementary school, he said upwards of 30 parents were either dropping off food or sending deliveries there daily, so the school set up a table in the foyer where students can go search for their bag at lunchtime.
A spokesperson for the Calgary Catholic School District said to their knowledge, St. Francis is the only school in its board addressing the matter.
In a statement, the Calgary Board of Education said it doesn’t have a specific policy on food deliveries, and it’s up to principals at individual schools to set guidelines if it is an issue.
“Students are discouraged from ordering deliveries into the building, though we are aware they may meet the driver in other locations on school property,” the statement said.
Students say it’s common, not necessarily an issue
Outside St. Francis, delivery driver Ali Nuru dropped off food for a student Tuesday. He says he’ll typically end up doing a couple of school deliveries a week.
“Most of the time I bring from McDonald's,” he said.
Delivery driver Ali Nuru says he typically delivers a couple of times a week to high schools, with McDonald's the No. 1 meal of choice. (Colleen Underwood/CBC)
Students said it’s fairly routine to see classmates meeting drivers in the parking lot to pick up their orders.

“A lot of times — I'm kind of snitching — but they'll be like, ‘oh can I go to the bathroom' and then they just go meet the driver around the school, like the front of the school and then bring the food in with them,” said Grade 11 student Rebira Assefa.
However, she said it hasn’t been a big deal in her classrooms, with most students unbothered by it.
The bathroom excuse can be an issue though, said Grade 11 student Bradley White, since only so many students are allowed out of a class at a time.
“Like if someone's out for too long, then the teacher will be like, ‘OK, no one's allowed to use the bathroom for the rest of class because this person ruined it for everyone,’” said White.
Plus, he said it can be a distraction when someone orders an “excessive” amount of food for themselves and their friends, and brings it into class.
Cracking down on it, though, could be tricky.

“I don't really know how they would enforce a policy where you're not allowed to order something, because kids are going to do it anyways. They'll end up rebelling because you put another policy in,” said Grade 12 student Alysa Utigard.
